_comment: Loco4CoCo arcade companion. Point at any account/event by editing this file only.

event._region_comment: Marketplace listings are filtered to this region. Offering a visitor a share they cannot attach wastes the five minutes we just spent with them.
event.title: Loco for CoCo
event.subtitle: Five minutes to your next data product
event._operator_comment: Who is running THIS stand, and which stand it is. Written to SESSIONS.SE_OPERATOR on every visitor. It was read by the server but never defined here, which is why all 52 existing rows have it empty. Set it per laptop before doors open: it cannot be reconstructed afterwards, and without it 'which stand produced the best conversations' is unanswerable. Format: 'Name / Stand label', e.g. 'P Gardner / Stand 2'.
event._byline_comment: Shown under the title on the start screen. Left EMPTY by default so a fresh cloner does not ship someone else's name at their own event. Set it to your own, or leave blank to show nothing.

coco._comment: Each message spawns `cortex exec`. Deliberately UNCAPPED - no max-turns, no effort floor, history left on. Cost is managed by observation (see cost_log) not by throttling the visitor.
coco.warm_agent_comment: Hold a `cortex mcp serve` process open between visitors. Measured ~3.4s per turn against ~26s for a cold `cortex exec`, because exec has no --resume/--session and pays ~18s of process startup every call. Strictly one in-flight call: concurrent calls on one process were proven to mis-correlate and return another call's answer. Set false to fall straight through to exec.
coco.turn_timeout_comment: Wall-clock ceiling per turn. The Library has been measured at a 127.3s outlier against a 2.2s median; past the ceiling the visitor is better served by the precomputed answer than a better sentence.

qa._comment: The QA bot reviews the finished blueprint before it is staged. Deterministic checks always run and silently repair what is fixable from the closed lists (off-list features dropped, guide fallback, readiness clamped, platforms re-normalised); each change is recorded to LOCO4COCO.BOOTH.QA_FINDINGS with before/after, and a summary lands on the SESSIONS row. model_review adds one fast COMPLETE call judging whether the POC addresses the visitor's stated problem - it fails open, never blocking the handover.

delivery._comment: Delivery is a QR code pointing at the visitor's .docx, staged and presigned on @LOCO4COCO.BOOTH.BLUEPRINTS (presign_seconds = 7 days). There is deliberately no email and no local record: email was removed (snowflake.com publishes DMARC p=reject, and the Gmail MCP cannot send or attach under `cortex exec`), so the old outbox that wrote visitor PII to disk on every visit was pure liability on a shared laptop and is gone. The governed Snowflake SESSIONS row is the only kept record of a visitor.

intake._comment: CoCo gets up and asks who the present is for. Typing is limited to these three fields plus any 'Other' answers.
intake.industry_question: And what world do you work in? I'll fill the library with the right shelves.
intake.confirm_industry: I'm guessing {industry} from {company} - have I got that right?

letter._comment: The opening is a sequence, not a form: CoCo is home, a letter arrives, and the letter itself IS the intake. Every phase is click-skippable so a booth operator is never trapped in an animation.
letter.arctic_sub: (Yes, penguins live in Antarctica, but CoCo is special!)
body: I've heard you and the Cortex Crew have been cooking up some amazing products recently.
Me and my team at {company} wanted to learn more.
We're particularly interested in {industry} and wanted to understand what a Proof of Concept (POC) would look like for this on Snowflake.
letter.line1: A letter, from my friend {first_name}! Better get to work...
letter.line2: Anyway, let's go and get this show on the road.
letter.map_line: First stop is my Data Library. That's where I keep all the unstructured, semi-structured and structured data that would be useful for {first_name} and {company}.
letter.bubble:
Wow, a letter from my friend! Shame I can't make out some of these words...
(Please fill this in with your details)

intake.problem_label: The problem you want to solve (two sentences)
intake.problem_placeholder: e.g. our engineers waste hours hunting through old inspection reports. We want answers in seconds, with the source.
intake._problem_placeholder_comment: intake.problem_placeholder is the fallback shown before an industry is chosen. Once one is picked, industries.<key>.problem_placeholder replaces it so the example belongs to the visitor's world.

healthcare.name: Healthcare & Life Sciences

data_sources.label: Patient records
data_sources.note: Structured clinical records in a PAS or EPR system

data_sources.label: Clinical notes & letters
data_sources.note: Free text - discharge summaries, referrals, correspondence

healthcare.problem_placeholder: e.g. our clinicians re-read discharge summaries to find one detail. We want the answer in seconds, with the source.

financial.name: Financial Services

data_sources.label: Regulatory reporting
data_sources.note: Submissions and the reconciliations behind them

financial.problem_placeholder: e.g. every complaint is read by hand to spot the urgent ones. We want them sorted and routed the moment they land.

retail.name: Retail & Consumer Goods

data_sources.label: Sales & till transactions
data_sources.note: Basket-level sales by store and channel

data_sources.label: Supplier & logistics data
data_sources.note: Purchase orders, lead times, delivery performance

data_sources.label: Reviews & customer service
data_sources.note: Free text feedback, returns reasons, contact logs

retail.problem_placeholder: e.g. nobody can say why a line sold out in one region and sat still in another. We want that answered without a data team.

public.name: Public Sector & Government

data_sources.label: Policy & guidance documents
data_sources.note: Years of PDFs, circulars and statutory guidance

public.problem_placeholder: e.g. our guidance sits in years of PDFs nobody can search. We want caseworkers to ask a question and get a cited answer.

manufacturing.name: Manufacturing & Industrial

data_sources.label: Machine & sensor telemetry
data_sources.note: High frequency readings off the line

data_sources.label: Maintenance logs
data_sources.note: Work orders and engineer free text

data_sources.label: Supplier & inbound logistics
data_sources.note: Component lead times and quality by supplier

data_sources.label: Energy consumption
data_sources.note: Meter data by line and site

manufacturing.problem_placeholder: e.g. we find out a machine was failing after it stopped. We want the warning while there is still time to act.

energy.name: Energy & Utilities

data_sources.label: Field engineer reports
data_sources.note: Free text inspection and repair notes

energy.problem_placeholder: e.g. engineer notes and meter data live apart, so we cannot connect a fault to what led to it. We want them joined up.

media.name: Media, Telco & Entertainment

data_sources.label: Viewing & listening events
data_sources.note: Play, pause, completion by title and device

media.problem_placeholder: e.g. we know what was watched but not why anyone churned. We want the two joined so we can see it coming.

other.name: Something else

data_sources.label: Core operational records
data_sources.note: Whatever your main system of record holds

data_sources.label: Documents & PDFs
data_sources.note: Years of unstructured files nobody can query

data_sources.label: Customer or member data
data_sources.note: Who you serve and what they have done

other.problem_placeholder: e.g. the answer exists somewhere in our systems and it takes days to get it out. We want it in seconds, with the source.

library.name: The Data Library
library.heading: Which of these do you work with at the moment?
library.hint: Tick everything that applies. Add your own if it's missing.
library.narrative: This is my magic data library, {first_name}. Every shelf can mimic something {company} already holds. You can ask me for anything, from MP3 to CSV, PDF to Parquet.
library.prompt:
The visitor works in {industry} at {company}. They described their problem as: "{problem}". In THE LIBRARY they said they already hold: {selection}, sitting on {platforms}. Reply in at most 2 short sentences: connect the most valuable thing in that list to the problem they described, and name ONE specific, named Snowflake feature that would unlock it (for example Cortex Analyst, Cortex Search, Snowpark, Dynamic Tables, ML Classification, Snowflake Marketplace). Name the feature, not a general ability like handling large datasets. Warm, plain English, no jargon, no bullet points, no headings, no em dashes.

Word choice matters: this goes into a document handed to a visitor at a public booth. Never use the words die, dies, dying, kill, killed, killing, suicide, cripple or crippled, and never use violent or morbid metaphors for systems failing. Say fails, stops, degrades or goes down instead. Keep the register plain and calm.

marketplace.name: The Marketplace
marketplace.heading: What shall we join to your data?
marketplace.hint: Live listings, filtered to what you can attach in this region. No ETL, no storage cost, always current. The same door works outwards: this is how you share your own data without handing over a copy.
marketplace.other_placeholder: e.g. UK postcode boundaries, company registry data
marketplace._discovery_comment: manual = serve the CURATED marketplace-index.md, which is what the offline agentic-search precompute produced: 6 verified, free, UK-weighted, importability-checked picks per industry. This is deliberate for a branded event. MEASURED with discovery='live': public sector returned three Met Office weather products plus 'India Economic Monitor', because live matching ranked raw keyword hits with no geography and pinned two weather listings; after adding geo weighting and per-industry avoid terms it returned only 4 results, two of them weak ('UN Codes for Trade and Transport', 'Overture Maps'). Curation beats liveness on a stand: the stall must be predictable and defensible. Set to 'live' to use SHOW AVAILABLE LISTINGS (region + is_ready_for_import + geo weighting + industry_avoid), falling back here below min_live_results.
marketplace.narrative: This is the Snowflake Marketplace, and every stall is a real company's data. You attach it and query it live, seconds later. You never copy it, you never build a pipeline for it, and you never pay to store it.
marketplace.prompt:
The visitor's stated problem is: "{problem}". Keep your answer pointed at it.
The visitor works in {industry} at {company} and holds: {held}. In THE MARKETPLACE they chose to join these real Snowflake Marketplace listings: {selection}. Reply in at most 2 short sentences: say what joining those lets them answer that they cannot answer today. Refer to the datasets only by the names given above; do not invent any other listing or provider name. Plain English, no bullet points, no em dashes.

Word choice matters: this goes into a document handed to a visitor at a public booth. Never use the words die, dies, dying, kill, killed, killing, suicide, cripple or crippled, and never use violent or morbid metaphors for systems failing. Say fails, stops, degrades or goes down instead. Keep the register plain and calm.

workshop.name: The Workshop
workshop.heading: What do we want our Proof of Concept to do?
workshop.hint: Think big and say it in one line. An AI agent that answers for you, a dashboard that explains itself, an app your team actually opens every morning, something that spots trouble before it lands. Whatever it is, we forge it here.
workshop.placeholder: e.g. an agent that answers policy questions with citations
workshop.narrative: Bench cleared, forge lit. Tell me what the finished thing does and I'll draw up the plan.
workshop.prompt:
The visitor's stated problem is: "{problem}". Keep your answer pointed at it.
The visitor is {first_name}, {industry}, at {company}. They hold: {held}. They will join: {joined}. In THE WORKSHOP they said the POC should: "{input}".

First choose the archetype that matches what they are ACTUALLY trying to do. Pick exactly one of these keys:
talk-to-my-data (ask questions of structured data in plain English)
ask-my-documents (search or Q&A over documents and free text)
extract-from-paperwork (pull structured fields out of forms, invoices, letters)
triage-and-classify (sort, route or prioritise incoming items)
an-agent-that-acts (takes an action, not just answers)
predict-what-happens-next (forecasting or risk scoring)
join-the-silos (unify data that lives in separate systems)
share-without-copying (give someone else live access)
watch-it-live (streaming or near real-time monitoring)

The data they hold decides this. If their source is documents or free text, it is ask-my-documents or extract-from-paperwork, NOT talk-to-my-data.

For features, you MUST choose 2 to 4 names EXACTLY as spelled from this list and nothing else:
{feature_list}

Return ONLY minified JSON, no prose and no code fence, with exactly these keys:
{"archetype": one key from the list above, "poc_name": short name in their own language, max 8 words, "features": array of 2-4 names copied exactly from the feature list, "reply": max 40 words, warm, spoken aloud to them, no bullet points, no em dashes}

Nothing else is wanted. Do NOT write a summary, considerations, a first step or a score - those are filled in elsewhere, and every extra word here is time the visitor spends waiting at the bench. Never claim the POC is built.

Word choice matters: this goes into a document handed to a visitor at a public booth. Never use the words die, dies, dying, kill, killed, killing, suicide, cripple or crippled, and never use violent or morbid metaphors for systems failing. Say fails, stops, degrades or goes down instead. Keep the register plain and calm.
workshop._tool_hint_comment: Set to e.g. 'Use your tools to check the Snowflake docs before choosing features.' to make the tray show real tool calls. Measured cost: about 34s for one lookup, so it is off by default. The Ask stop is the budgeted place for tool use.

postbox.name: The Postbox
postbox.heading: Shall I post it?
postbox.hint: I'll write it up properly and put it in the post.
postbox.narrative: Wrapped, labelled and ready. Say the word and I'll put it in your hands.

intro.title: Loco for CoCo
body: This is a fun way to experience the power of Cortex Code (CoCo) through the medium of an arcade game.

You have 5 minutes to explore what building a Proof of Concept on Snowflake really looks like, with CoCo as your guide to our features, marketplace datasets, and how enterprise-grade AI can bring your ideas to life.
You will leave with a personalised action plan for building it for real. Be daring, this is a flexible process with a genuinely useful outcome.
*Anything you type stays private*, only shared with you and Snowflake.

ask._comment: The one unscripted stop. Always exec (never the fast path): this is where real CoCo earns it, because nothing is injected for it to reflect back, so it has a genuine reason to use its tools. Optional and skippable so it cannot blow the five minutes.
ask.heading: Ask CoCo one thing
ask.hint: Optional. One question about your POC and CoCo will look it up properly.
ask.placeholder: e.g. what would we need before we could trust the predictions?
ask.tool_hint: Use your tools to check the Snowflake documentation before you answer, so the answer is grounded rather than guessed. One lookup is enough.
ask._status: Disabled: it must be a deliberate beat in the flow, not a popup. The /api/ask endpoint and the card are built and proven (real tool call, grounded answer) - re-enable when it has its own step or tile.

marketplace._comment: Live discovery needs NO private preview: SHOW AVAILABLE LISTINGS piped through RESULT_SCAN gives 188 importable listings in AWS_EU_WEST_2 (of 4327 total, 799 region-available). Measured 2026-08-17. The curated index stays as the offline-safe fallback.

agentic._comment: Tier 0, ahead of live. Built and end-to-end tested on PG_LONDON 2026-08-23, then DISABLED the same day: measured latency 70-110s+ (2 of 3 runs timed out) is too high and too variable to trust against an unmeasured Library dwell time (see BOOTH-RUNBOOK.md). Replaced for now by a precompute pass instead - the same PrPr agentic search run offline, once, to add a verified 6th free-weighted pick per industry to marketplace-index.md (Tier 2). Code left in place and dormant; re-enable once real Library timing data exists or latency improves. No cap by design if re-enabled: an SE watches spend in cost.jsonl (kind=marketplace_agentic) and flips enabled back off by hand if needed.

marketplace._pinned_comment: Verified importable in AWS_EU_WEST_2 on 2026-08-17. Met Office profile GZTDZJKVBD. Surfaced first when the live tier finds them. Ordnance Survey is deliberately absent: it is NOT on the Marketplace in any region, so it lives in config.sourcing instead.

provider_names._comment: SHOW AVAILABLE LISTINGS returns an opaque profile id, not a display name.

marketplace._exclude_comment: Keyword matching pulls in tools and apps, not just data. A healthcare stall offering 'Snowflake Health Check Dashboard' reads as broken, so obvious non-dataset titles are dropped.
marketplace._geo_comment: The event is a UK stand, so a UK visitor must not be offered 'India Economic Monitor' or 'All International Postal Codes' ahead of the ONS census. `prefer` terms score a listing UP, `demote` terms score it DOWN, and keyword matches are ranked by that score instead of catalogue order. Change these when the event moves country - nothing here is hardcoded.
marketplace._avoid_comment: Per-industry veto. The public-sector keyword 'postcode' was matching 'Postcode Sector Weather Forecasts' - a weather product - so three of the six public-sector picks were Met Office. These terms drop a listing from an industry even when a keyword hit.

sourcing._comment: Where data can come from when the visitor is NOT yet a Snowflake customer. Ordnance Survey lives here rather than in the Marketplace because it is not listed there in any region (checked 2026-08-17); Open UPRN exists but is not available in AWS_EU_WEST_2.
sourcing.synthetic_hint: CoCo can mimic any shelf as synthetic data so a POC can start before the real feed exists. Generate it in Snowflake with GENERATOR and RANDOM, or let Cortex fabricate realistic rows from a description.

external.name: Ordnance Survey Data Hub
external.note: UK geospatial: addresses, UPRN, topography. Not on the Snowflake Marketplace.

external.name: Met Office DataHub
external.note: Direct API access, and also on the Marketplace.

platforms._comment: Where the data lives today. Asked on CoCo's home stage (moved out of the library 2026-08-25), one tap; decides the integration-path section of the blueprint.
platforms.heading: Where does {company} keep its data today?
platforms.hint: Tap every platform it sits on. This is what decides how we get it into Snowflake.
platforms._guardrail: `exclusive` chips cannot be combined with a named source: "Already in Snowflake" prints "nothing to move" and "Not sure yet" prints "go and ask", so pairing either with Oracle or AWS made the blueprint contradict itself. The UI clears the other group on tap and the server re-normalises, so a bypassed UI cannot produce a contradictory document. `max_routes` caps the ingestion section: 8 chips printed 8 route paragraphs and 5 Openflow mentions, which read as a template rather than a plan.
platforms._exclusive_comment: Only "Not sure yet" is exclusive, because it is the absence of an answer rather than an answer. "Already in Snowflake" is deliberately NOT exclusive: an organisation can have data in Snowflake AND in Oracle, and forcing a choice made the visitor misrepresent their estate. When it is combined with a named source the blueprint prints a combined route (see PLATFORM_COMBINED in server.py) rather than "nothing to move".

country._comment: Home-stage question 2. Europe-weighted for London/Paris. Frames the residency follow-up.
country.heading: And where is {company} based?
country.hint: Tap every country you have a base in. It helps me keep your data where your rules need it.

residency._comment: Home-stage question 3. Sovereignty-framed. {country} is interpolated from the country answer; falls back to 'your country'.
residency.heading: Where are {company}'s data and AI models allowed to run?
residency.hint: Tap every one that applies. This shapes the region we build in, and it goes in your blueprint.
options_template: Anywhere in the EU is fine

sovereignty._comment: Visitor-facing sovereignty copy. react.* are CoCo's one-liners on the home stage, keyed by the answer. pillars.* are reused verbatim in the blueprint's Sovereignty & security section. Kept here so Paris is a copy swap.

react.platform_already: Perfect - it's already in Snowflake, so we skip the plumbing and go straight to building.
react.platform_unsure: No problem - we'll work the plumbing out together, it's usually the easy part.
react.platform_named: Good - I know exactly how to get data out of {platform} and into Snowflake, in region and without copying it around.
react.country: {country}, lovely. I'll keep everything where {country}'s rules need it.
react.residency_country_only: Understood - everything stays in {country}. Your data, the AI models, all of it.
react.residency_eu: Great - we'll keep it inside the EU. Data and models both, no border crossings.
react.residency_us_ok: Plenty of room to work with, then - and it still stays wherever you choose.
react.residency_unsure: We'll keep it close to home by default - you can always widen it later.

pillars.data: Your data never leaves {region}: it stays in your own Snowflake account, in region, not copied out to be processed.
pillars.models: Cortex runs the AI models where your data already lives, so nothing crosses a border to be understood.
pillars.marketplace: Marketplace data is shared live rather than copied, and you are only ever offered listings available in {region}.
pillars.governance: One set of controls - role-based access, masking, row-level policies - governs all of it, in one place.

sovereignty._summary_comment: Spoken over the house scene after the letter is submitted. CoCo reads back what was given, then makes the security and AI point inside that summary rather than as a separate beat. Placeholders: {first_name}, {company_bit}, {industry_bit}, {platform_bit}, {region}. The _bit placeholders are assembled by the client from what the visitor actually supplied, so a missing answer leaves no dangling sentence. Each line auto-advances on a timer scaled to its length.
summary: So, {first_name}, let me make sure I have this. {company_bit}{industry_bit}{platform_bit}I have the problem you want to solve, and that is the bit everything else hangs off.

Here is the part that matters before we start building. All of this happens inside your own Snowflake account in {region}. Your data does not get copied out to be processed, and the AI models run where the data already lives, so nothing crosses a border to be understood.

And the question I get asked most, so I will answer it now. What you send the AI stays yours. Your prompts, your data and the answers are never used to train external models, and they never leave your account. One set of controls governs all of it, the same ones you already use.
You will not have to move house for any of it either. Snowflake talks to what you already run, and with Iceberg your tables stay in open formats other engines can read, so there is no one way door.
